title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text: Handwriting is personal, and examiners have long used it to judge who wrote a document. Reviews of writer identification describe how the field moved from hand-made features to machine learning and, more recently, deep learning (Rehman et al., 2019). Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn features straight from the pixels and have been used to identify writers from images of their handwriting (Gu et al., 2018; He & Schomaker, 2019). A second route treats the problem as similarity learning: instead of naming the writer, a Siamese network judges whether two samples came from the same hand, so it can be applied to writers it has not seen (Chicco, 2021). This report builds both models on simulated images of the digits 0 to 4 written by 20 writers. We explore the data (Task 1), fit a CNN that identifies the writer (Task 2), fit a Siamese network that verifies whether two images share a writer (Task 3), explain how the data were split and how leakage was avoided (Task 4), tune the CNN (Task 5) and compare the two models (Task 6).

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
2.1 Data Overview
The data consisted of 25,000 greyscale images of 28 x 28 pixels, showing the digits 0 to 4. Each of the 20 writers wrote each digit 50 times (replicate) in each of the 5 sessions, giving a total of 1,250 images per writer. The original pixel values [0,255], were scaled to [0, 1] before fitting the neural network models, because inputs on a small common scale make gradient-based training more stable (Chollet et al., 2022; Goodfellow et al., 2016). The metadata contains the image ID, writer ID, digit, session number and replicate number. To explore the sources of variability in the data, four analyses were carried out including variation between writers, variation across sessions for a subset of writers, variation within sessions (across replicates) for a subset of writers, and a quantitative comparison of the three using pixel distances.

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
2.2 Variation between writers
To examine variation between writers, each digit was plotted for all 20 writers, with session and replicate fixed at 1. This produced five plots, one per digit. Writer-identification methods rely on the fact that people differ in features such as size, shape and slant (Rehman et al., 2019), so we looked for these features. Figure 1 shows clear differences in handwriting style between the 20 writers.


Show code
plot_writers(0)
plot_writers(1)











(a) Digit 0











(b) Digit 1






Figure 1: Digits 0 and 1 for all 20 writers, with session 1 and replicate 1 fixed.




Variation in shape is most clearly observed in digits 0 and 1 (Figure 1). For example, although all the 1s have a base, some have a hook at the top (writers 1, 7 and 14), while others have a curved body that resembles the digit 2 (writers 3, 9 and 17). For digit 0, shapes vary from round to oval, and some writers (10, 12, 13 and 19) draw squarer shapes with a flat top. The remaining digits follow a more consistent style, with the primary differences being slant and size. Size also varies whereby some writers (3 and 9) write small and compact digits, while others fill the space with large digits. Slant varies from upright to a rightward slant (writers 18 and 10), while writer 19 slants to the left. These differences in size, shape and slant are features that the models could learn. The plots for digits 2, 3 and 4 are in Figure 15 (Appendix A).

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
2.3 Variation across sessions
To assess whether a person’s handwriting changes between sessions, 10 writers were randomly sampled and each digit was plotted across the 5 sessions, with the replicate fixed at 1. The plots for digits 2, 3 and 4 are in Figure 16 (Appendix A).


Show code
plot_sessions_sample(1)
plot_sessions_sample(0)











(a) Digit 1











(b) Digit 0






Figure 2: Digits 1 and 0 for ten randomly sampled writers (seed 1), with replicate 1 fixed. Rows are writers and columns are sessions 1 to 5.




There are visible changes in style between sessions, and these are more noticeable for some writers than for others. Although some changes are noticeable, some writers remained consistent in certain characteristics. For example, writer 3 wrote small digits in all sessions and, for digit 1, kept their signature hook in every session, as writer 17 did. Other writers changed their characteristic style, for example, writer 19 slanted the digits slightly to the left in the first session, but the digits became more upright as the sessions progressed. Writer 1’s 1s also changed between sessions because some have hooks and the lengths of the strokes differ. This indicates that a writer’s handwriting may change between sessions. Although some of these changes are minor, they alter a writer’s characteristic style from session 1, so the models may identify some writers less accurately in a new session.

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
2.4 Variation across replicates


Show code
plot_replicates(1)








Figure 3: Digit 1 for the same ten writers as in the sessions figure, with session 1 fixed and replicates 1, 11, 21, 31 and 41. Rows are writers and columns are replicates.





To assess whether handwriting style drifted across replicates within a session, the same 10 writers were used, with replicates 1, 11, 21, 31 and 41 plotted for session 1 (fixed). The digits were near-identical across the replicates, with little to no change in style. This indicates that a writer’s handwriting within one session is usually the same. The plots for digits 0, 2, 3 and 4 are in Figure 17 (Appendix A).

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
2.5 Quantifying the variation
To quantify the variation between writers, across sessions and within sessions, the Euclidean distance between two images was computed over all 784 pixels. For a sample of 1,000 draws, the function picked a writer, a digit, two sessions and two replicates and formed three comparisons with the digit matched within a session (comparing replicates), across sessions (the same writer) and between writers. The three distances were compared with a Friedman test, followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm’s adjustment for the three comparisons. We also report the paired effect size dz, the mean of the paired differences divided by their standard deviation (Goulet-Pelletier & Cousineau, 2018). Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals from 2000 resamples of the draws (Efron & Hastie, 2016).
Two images of the same digit by the same writer in the same session were near identical (mean distance = 2.72, SD = 0.50), which indicates that the 50 replicates are near copies of one another. The across-session distance for the same writer had a mean of 7.15 and SD = 1.63. The highest variation was recorded between different writers (mean distance = 8.59, SD = 1.14) (Table 1, Figure 4). The three distances differ clearly in the matched draws (Friedman chi-squared = 1652.9 on 2 df, p < 1e-16; Kendall’s W = 0.83), and all three Holm-adjusted pairwise tests give p < 1e-16 (Table 2).

Figure 4: Distribution of pixel distances by comparison type.





With 1,000 draws almost any difference would be significant, so the effect sizes are more informative than the p-values. The across-session minus within-session gap is 4.43 (95% CI 4.33 to 4.53; dz = 2.72), whereas the between-writer minus across-session gap is only 1.44 (95% CI 1.33 to 1.56; dz = 0.77). In practical terms, a change of session moves a writer’s digit about 75% of the way to where a different writer’s digit sits ((7.15 − 2.72) / (8.59 − 2.72)). A writer is therefore only partly recognisable from the pixels of a single image, and any model has to cope with the same person looking different from one session to the next.

The ratio of across-session to within-session distance was above 1 for every digit, and its confidence interval never came near 1 (Figure 5, Table 3). It was highest for digit 1 (3.40; within-session distance 2.01) and lowest for digit 4 (2.36). Digit 1 is a thin stroke, so a small shift in position or slant changes which pixels are lit, which is a plausible reason for its larger ratio, although this was not tested. Digit 0 ranked third of the five digits (ratio 2.56). Pixel distance is a crude measure, because a small shift in a digit’s position can inflate the distance between two images of the same shape, so these numbers describe the data and do not by themselves show how well a model can separate writers.

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
3.2 What Task 2 tells us
The CNN fitted the training sessions almost perfectly (98.5% accuracy after 10 epochs) but identified the writer correctly in only 57.9% of the test images from the unseen session 5 (Table 5). The exact Clopper-Pearson interval is 56.5% to 59.2%, but this treats the 5 000 images as independent, which they are not. The cluster bootstrap, which resamples whole writer-digit groups, gives a much wider interval of 48.9% to 66.9% (Saravanan et al., 2020), so the honest statement is that test accuracy is roughly 49% to 67%. Either way it is far above the 5% expected by chance, and far below the training accuracy. The learning curves show where the gap comes from (Figure 6). Validation accuracy stays between about 45% and 55% from the first epoch, while the validation loss rises from 1.78 to 4.22 as the training loss falls. The network is becoming more confident without becoming more correct on a new session, which is what overfitting looks like (Goodfellow et al., 2016). We did not use early stopping here, so the test result is for the model after 10 epochs.
The random split is the contrast that matters. The same network reached 99.4% validation accuracy within ten epochs when the images were shuffled across training and validation. That near-perfect score is not evidence of a better model. It is the leakage that Task 1 predicted, because the validation images have near-copies in the training set (the within-session distance was only 2.72). The gap of about 42 points between the random split (99.4%) and the session-split test (57.9%) shows how much a random split would have overstated performance (Roberts et al., 2017; Saeb et al., 2017).
Accuracy was similar across digits (51.1% to 67.0%), with digit 3 highest at 67.0%. The cluster-bootstrap intervals for the five digits overlap almost completely (Figure 7, Table 6), and a Friedman test across digits with writers as blocks gives chi-squared = 1.17 on 4 df, p = 0.88 (Kendall’s W = 0.01). The data therefore give little support for saying that some digits identify writers better than others, and the digit 3 result should be treated as a hint at most.
The errors are concentrated in particular writers more than in particular digits (Figure 8, Figure 9). The clearest case is writer 10: 241 of that writer’s 250 test images (96%) were assigned to writer 2 (Table 7). Writer 5 was mistaken for writer 13 in 61% of cases, and writer 13 for writer 5 in 40%, so those two seem to write alike in session 5. We only report this as an observation, because the matrix shows that it happens but not why.
In real-world terms, the model is given one digit from a known writer in a session it has not seen and must say who wrote it. The overall test accuracy of 57.9% means that, out of 100 new digits from known writers, about 58 are assigned to the right writer and about 42 to the wrong one, so the model has learned real writer information but still makes many mistakes. The results do not show how it would handle writers it has not seen, since it can only choose among the 20 known writers, or real handwriting, since the images are simulated.

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
4.1 Pair construction


Show code
seed_all(1)   

# 1. Split by WRITER first, so validation/test writers are never seen in training
tr_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 1:14)
va_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 15:17)
te_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 18:20)

# 2. Build pairs INSIDE one part. About half are same-writer (label 1), half
#    different-writer (label 0). Both images in a pair show the SAME digit, so
#    the model has to compare handwriting, not digit shape.
make_pairs <- function(ids, n){
  a <- sample(ids, n, replace = TRUE)
  same <- runif(n) < 0.5
  b <- integer(n)
  for (k in seq_len(n)){
    i <- a[k]
    pool <- ids[meta$digit[ids] == meta$digit[i]]
    pool <- if (same[k]) pool[meta$person_id[pool] == meta$person_id[i]]
            else         pool[meta$person_id[pool] != meta$person_id[i]]
    pool <- setdiff(pool, i)
    b[k] <- pool[sample.int(length(pool), 1)]
  }
  cbind(a, b)
}
make_batch <- function(p) list(
  left  = x[p[, 1], , , , drop = FALSE],
  right = x[p[, 2], , , , drop = FALSE],
  y     = matrix(as.numeric(meta$person_id[p[, 1]] == meta$person_id[p[, 2]]), ncol = 1))

tr_pairs <- make_pairs(tr_ids, 8000)
va_pairs <- make_pairs(va_ids, 2000)
te_pairs <- make_pairs(te_ids, 2000)   # keep the indices so test pairs can be analysed later
train <- make_batch(tr_pairs)
valid <- make_batch(va_pairs)
test  <- make_batch(te_pairs)




Show code

Show code
seed_all(1)   # fixed start weights and batch order for the Siamese network
# 3. Shared encoder: the same layers (same weights) are used for both images
img_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
z <- img_in |>
  layer_conv_2d(16, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
  layer_conv_2d(32, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_global_average_pooling_2d() |>
  layer_dense(16)
encoder <- keras_model(img_in, z)

# 4. Siamese model: output = Euclidean distance between the two embeddings
left_in  <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
right_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
emb_left  <- encoder(left_in)
emb_right <- encoder(right_in)
distance  <- op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(emb_left - emb_right), axis = 2, keepdims = TRUE) + 1e-7)
siamese <- keras_model(list(left_in, right_in), distance)


# 5. Contrastive loss with margin 1:
#    same pairs (y = 1) are pulled together (loss D^2);
#    different pairs (y = 0) are pushed apart until D >= 1, then left alone.
contrastive_loss <- function(y, d) {
  op_mean(y * op_square(d) + (1 - y) * op_square(op_maximum(1 - d, 0)))
}
siamese |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3), loss = contrastive_loss)

history_siam <- siamese |> fit(
  list(train$left, train$right), train$y,
  validation_data = list(list(valid$left, valid$right), valid$y),
  epochs = 12, batch_size = 64, verbose = 2,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 2,
                                           restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
4.2 Threshold, test performance and breakdowns


Show code
# 6. Choose the distance threshold on VALIDATION pairs (not on test)
valid_distance <- as.numeric(predict(siamese, list(valid$left, valid$right), verbose = 0))
valid_same <- valid$y[, 1] == 1

# balanced accuracy = average of (true match rate) and (true non-match rate)
bal_acc <- function(d, same, cut){
  pred_same <- d < cut
  (mean(pred_same[same]) + mean(!pred_same[!same])) / 2
}
# AUC = P(a same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a different-writer pair)
auc_dist <- function(d, same){
  r <- rank(d); n1 <- sum(same); n0 <- sum(!same)
  1 - (sum(r[same]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
4.3 What Task 3 tells us
On three writers the network never saw during training, the Siamese network separated same-writer from different-writer pairs well. At the distance threshold of 0.57 chosen on the validation pairs, balanced accuracy on the test pairs was 0.931 (95% bootstrap CI 0.919 to 0.942), with a true match rate of 0.923 and a true non-match rate of 0.939 (Table 9, Table 10). The AUC of 0.984 (95% CI 0.980 to 0.988) shows that the ranking of pairs by distance is good over all thresholds, not only at the one chosen (Figure 13, Figure 12). Early stopping kept the weights from epoch 4 (validation loss 0.104) and stopped at epoch 6 (Figure 10). The test balanced accuracy is higher than the 0.878 seen on the validation pairs at the chosen threshold. With only three writers in each of the two sets, that difference could come from which writers happened to be in each set, so we do not read anything into it.
Task 1 predicted that pairs from different sessions would be harder, and the session breakdown shows this for same-writer pairs (Table 11). Of the 200 same-writer pairs from the same session, 200 were accepted (100%, exact CI 98.2% to 100%), against 90.2% (681 of 755) for same-writer pairs from different sessions (Fisher exact p = 1.9e-08). For different-writer pairs there was no clear session effect (92.5% against 94.2%, p = 0.4). In other words, the network is least sure when asked to connect two sessions of one person, which is the case the application cares about. The same-session figure is also not independent evidence, since those images are near-copies.
Performance differed a little between the three test writers (balanced accuracy 0.963, 0.925 and 0.903 for writers 18, 19 and 20; Table 12), and between digits (Figure 14). With three writers and the pairs sharing images (2 000 test pairs use 2 475 distinct images, Table 8), the intervals in Table 9 are likely to be too narrow, so they should be read as the lower bound on the uncertainty.

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
7.1 What the two models measure
The CNN does identification: given one image it picks one of 20 known writers, so chance is 5%. The Siamese network does verification: given two images it decides whether one writer wrote both, so chance is 50%, and the test writers were never seen in training (Chicco, 2021). The results in Table 15 therefore answer different questions and should not be ranked against each other. The CNN named the right writer for 57.9% of the session 5 images, about 12 times chance, and the Siamese network reached a balanced accuracy of 0.931 with an AUC of 0.984. Choosing between two outcomes is easier than choosing among 20, so the higher Siamese score does not mean that it recognises writers better. The uncertainty also differs. The CNN interval comes from a cluster bootstrap that resamples writer-digit groups, which respects the dependence between near-copy images (Saravanan et al., 2020). The Siamese intervals resample pairs that share images, so they are too narrow and are best read as a lower bound. The cluster bootstrap itself can be conservative when the data are closer to independent than assumed (Saravanan et al., 2020), so the CNN interval errs on the side of being too wide, which is the safer mistake here.

In Task 1 we expected digits 0 and 1, which vary most in shape (Section 2), to carry the most writer information. The rankings do not clearly support this: digit 3 ranked best on average, while digits 0 and 1 had mean ranks of 3.33 and 2.00. Table 16 puts the digit results side by side. From highest to lowest, the CNN test accuracy ranks the digits 3, 0, 1, 4 and 2, the mean validation accuracy over the nine tuning settings ranks them 3, 1, 2, 0 and 4, and the Siamese balanced accuracy ranks them 1, 3, 4, 0 and 2. After averaging the three ranks, digit 3 comes out best (mean rank 1.33), and digit 0 is the least stable, moving over 2 places between the rankings. For the Siamese network, digit 1 scored highest (0.979) and digit 2 lowest (0.880), although the pairs are not independent, so these intervals are optimistic (Figure 14).
The evidence that digits differ is weaker than the rankings suggest. For the CNN test accuracy, a Friedman test with writers as blocks gave chi-squared = 1.17 on 4 df, p = 0.88 (Kendall’s W = 0.01), and the bootstrap intervals overlap almost completely. Across the nine tuning settings the ordering of digits was more consistent (Friedman chi-squared = 28.7 on 4 df, p = 8.9e-06; W = 0.80). However, those nine models share the same training and validation images, so this shows a stable ordering within one data set and not that it would reappear for new writers. The pixel distances of Task 1 did not predict the ranking either: digit 1 had the largest across-session to within-session ratio (3.40), yet it ranked third for CNN test accuracy and first for the Siamese network. Taken together, digit 3 carried the most writer information in this data set, every digit carried far more than chance, and the differences between digits are small next to the differences between writers (Figure 8).

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
section: 7.3 How a change of session affects performance
text:
7.3 How a change of session affects performance
Task 1 showed that a change of session moves a writer’s digit about 75% of the way towards another writer’s digit, and both models paid for it. The CNN fitted its training sessions to 98.5% and the randomly split validation images to 99.4%, where near copies were in the training set. On the new sessions it reached 54.5% (session 4) and 57.9% (session 5), a drop of about 41 points from training. The session 4 accuracy lies inside the session 5 bootstrap interval, so the two held-out sessions cannot be told apart. The validation loss rose from 1.78 to 4.22 while the training loss fell, which is the usual sign of overfitting (Goodfellow et al., 2016).
The Siamese network shows the same effect more precisely. All 200 same-writer pairs from one session were accepted, against 90.2% of the 755 same-writer pairs from different sessions (Fisher exact p = 1.9e-08; Table 11). Different-writer pairs showed no clear session effect (92.5% against 94.2%, p = 0.4). A change of session therefore caused false rejections of the same writer and not false matches. The Fisher test treats pairs as independent, so its p-value is too small, but the gap is large. The drops (about 41 points for the CNN and 9.8 points in the Siamese true match rate) cannot be compared directly because the tasks and writers differ. Their direction agrees with the evidence that testing on near copies of the training data overstates performance (Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023; Roberts et al., 2017; Saeb et al., 2017).

title: STA5073Z Assignment 2: Writer identification from handwritten digits
text:
7.4 Limitations and summary
The data are simulated, the CNN result rests on one held-out session, and the Siamese result rests on three writers. Each model was trained once with a fixed seed, so seed-to-seed variation was not measured. The nine tuning settings spanned 5.3 percentage points, and with 5 000 validation images the binomial standard error of an accuracy near 51.7% is about 0.7 points before dependence is allowed for, so differences of one or two points between settings should not be interpreted. The two models were also not compared on the same footing. A fairer test would score both on the same pairs, for example by using the CNN’s hidden layer as an embedding.
In summary, a CNN trained on sessions 1 to 3 identified the writer in 57.9% of the images from a new session, far above the 5% chance level but well below its training accuracy. A Siamese network separated same-writer from different-writer pairs of unseen writers with a balanced accuracy of 0.931. Digit 3 carried the most writer information, but the differences between digits were small. A change of session lowered performance in both models, mainly by making the same writer look like a different one.
